read: full: main text pp.1-16 (abstract, introduction, Sec. 2 methods and data annotation, Sec. 3 results, Sec. 4 discussion, Sec. 5 related work, Sec. 6 conclusion) and appendices B, C and E (pp.25-28); appendix A examples, appendix D (out-of-distribution details) and references skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2211.14275v1, 25 Nov 2022 (page 1 footer; DeepMind). The text shows no conference or workshop venue.
what_it_is: A DeepMind training study, not a benchmark. It compares outcome-based supervision (final-answer correctness only) with process-based supervision (GSM8K's human-written traces as SFT targets; human step labels for a process reward model) for a 70B base LM (Hoffmann et al., 2022) on GSM8K, across few-shot prompting, SFT, reward-model reranking and RL by expert iteration (pp.2-6). It defines 'trace error', the share of final-answer-correct solutions that contain at least one incorrect step as judged by human annotators (p.3). Outcome and process supervision reach similar final-answer error (23.5% vs 22.3% without a reward model; p.2, Table 1 p.7), but low trace error needs process feedback or a reward model that emulates it: 12.4% trace error for Few-shot+Final-Answer RL with ORM reranking against 4.4% and 3.5% for SFT with ORM or PRM reranking (p.8; Table 1 p.7). Its best system lowers final-answer error from the prior 16.8% to 12.7% and trace error from the prior 14.0% to 3.4% (abstract p.1; Table 1 p.7).
domain: grade-school math word problems (GSM8K); out-of-distribution check on the MATH pre-algebra split (p.11)
size: GSM8K split into 7,118 train, 256 validation and 1,319 test problems (p.3); PRM training labels on 1,560 model samples from 530 problems, 9,856 step labels (p.6); trace error estimated on 200 correct-answer problems per model for 10 models, double-labelled (p.6); one 70B base LM in several training variants (Table 1, p.7)
source_of_items: existing dataset (GSM8K problems and its human-written solutions); step labels written by qualified human annotators on model samples
has_gold_traces: partial: GSM8K's human-written reasoning traces are SFT targets and are shown to annotators (pp.4, 6); step correctness is human-labelled because the authors 'lack reliable programmatic means for determining the correctness of intermediate steps' (p.4)
evaluation: final answer (exact string match on integer answers) plus human step-level evaluation of correct-answer solutions (first major mistake, aggregated as trace error), reported with a min-max range over the two raters (pp.3, 6; Table 1 p.7)
human_validation: Annotators had to pass a qualification on solutions where three authors agreed on the first major mistake; 21 of 91 candidates were admitted (p.25). Ratings from 4 of 21 annotators with under 75% agreement on doubly rated problems were removed, 21% of the training labels (pp.25-26). After this, training-set agreement was 92% with Cohen's kappa 0.915 on locating the first incorrect step; on the evaluation set agreement was 87% with Cohen's kappa 0.34 on whether a full trace is correct, lower because for correct-answer solutions 'whether or not an intermediate step is incorrect can be more subtle' (p.26). Trace-error estimates carry wide rater ranges, e.g. 3.4 (0.0-6.8) (Table 1, p.7).

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in May. It is the first empirical comparison of process- and outcome-based supervision ('to our knowledge this is the first empirical paper to discuss it', p.13) and the origin of the quantity EngTrace's X1 hard case measures: the share of correct-answer traces that contain an incorrect step (trace error, p.3; EngTrace: 93 of 228 correct-answer traces, state brief section 3). Its authors fell back on human step labels because no programmatic check of intermediate steps existed for GSM8K (p.4); EngTrace's template-computed intermediate values supply such a check in its domain. It also expects outcome and process feedback to align more closely in math than in other domains (Sec. 4.2, p.13), which EngTrace can test in engineering. The search note's summary ('trace error among answer-correct solutions cut from 14.0% to 3.4% only with process supervision') is wrong twice: 14.0% is a prior system (PaLM-540B few-shot, from other papers) and 3.4% is SFT+ORM-RL, which uses an outcome-supervised reward model (Table 1, p.7). Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity; it can also support the introduction's claim that a correct answer does not certify the steps.

suggested_wording: Process supervision was first compared with outcome supervision by Uesato et al. (2022), who found on GSM8K that the two reach similar final-answer error but that low trace error, the share of correct answers reached through an incorrect step as judged by human annotators, requires process feedback or a reward model that emulates it.
facts_to_cite: First comprehensive comparison of process- and outcome-based supervision on a natural-language task, GSM8K (abstract p.1; p.13)
Defines trace error as the fraction of problems with correct final answers for which the solution contains at least one incorrect reasoning step, estimated by human annotation (p.3)
Outcome- and process-based approaches reach similar final-answer error: 23.5% vs 22.3% without a reward model and 16.6% vs 14.8% with one (p.2; Table 1 p.7)

Low trace error requires process feedback or a reward model that emulates it: Few-shot+Final-Answer RL with ORM reranking has 12.4% trace error against 4.4% and 3.5% for SFT with ORM or PRM reranking; training against an ORM instead of final-answer correctness lowers it to 5.5% (p.8; Table 1 p.7)
Best results improve on prior work from 16.8% to 12.7% final-answer error and from 14.0% to 3.4% trace error (abstract p.1; Table 1 p.7)
Step labels came from humans because the authors 'lack reliable programmatic means for determining the correctness of intermediate steps' (p.4)
Human agreement on whether a correct-answer trace is fully correct was 87% with Cohen's kappa 0.34, against kappa 0.915 for locating the first error on the training set (p.26)
The authors expect process- and outcome-based feedback to align more closely for math than for other domains (Sec. 4.2, p.13)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the target quantity (incorrect steps behind correct answers; EngTrace's X1 hard case, 93 of 228 correct-answer traces with an incorrect step, 175 of the 178 incorrect steps calculation slips) and human step-level judgement of model traces. Lacks: engineering (GSM8K only); generated instances (static public set, no contamination measure); gold intermediate values a program can check (p.4); a validated automatic step evaluator (its PRM is a training signal judged by downstream error); it is a training study, not a benchmark. Uesato's annotators mark only the first 'major mistake' (p.6), whereas EngTrace's experts label every step, so the two trace-error figures are not like for like. Its evaluation-set agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.34 on whole-trace correctness, p.26) is a different statistic from EngTrace's Fleiss kappa 0.781 on step labels and should not be set against it directly.
notes: Internal inconsistency to avoid repeating: the conclusion (p.15) says 'SFT with PRM reranking reduces the state-of-the-art trace error rate from 14.0% to 3.4%, while its outcome-based analogue achieves 12.7%' and that ORM-based RL reduces trace error 'from 12.7% to 5.5%', but Table 1 (p.7) gives 3.5% for SFT with PRM reranking, 3.4% for SFT+ORM-RL and 12.4% for the outcome-based Few-shot+Final-Answer RL with ORM reranking, and 12.7% is a final-answer error. Cite Table 1's figures. The 14.0% baseline is PaLM-540B few-shot taken from other papers (Table 1, p.7), not a model trained here. Trace-error estimates are noisy (min-max rater ranges, Table 1). The search note mentions a NeurIPS 2022 MATH-AI workshop version that the text does not show; cite as arXiv 2022 unless that venue is confirmed.
